    Introduction to stcsanalysis

    Jaromil Frossard

    introduction-to-stcsanalysis.Rmd

    0. Introduction

    This tutorial presents the main functionality of the stcsanalysis package. It shows how tailored tables and utility functions work together to help data-management and statistical analysis.

    1. Installation

    The appropriate version of stcsanalysis depends on the version of the AT. The latest version of the stcsanalysis like so:

    remotes::install_github("swiss-transplant-cohort-study/stcsanalysis")

    2. Load package and data

    First, stcsanalysis and other data analysis packages are loaded:

    library(stcsanalysis)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(survival)
#> Warning: package 'survival' was built under R version 4.4.3

    Once the path to the STCS data-cut is assigned to stcsat_dir (eg: stcsat_dir = "path/to/stcs/data-cut/folder/csv/"), the data can be loaded as follows:

    stcs <- stcs_read(stcsat_dir)

    3. Data-cut overview

    3.1 stcs object

    The stcs object is a named list of tibble objects. The names of the loaded tables can be retrieved as follows:

    names(stcs)
#>  [1] "admin"               "allcancerstatus"     "biopsyrejection"    
#>  [4] "biosample"           "biosampleusage"      "careprovider"       
#>  [7] "consent"             "donor"               "donorhla"           
#> [10] "donorserology"       "deathcause"          "graftloss"          
#> [13] "graftlosscause"      "hcplog"              "immunologyantihla"  
#> [16] "immunologycm"        "immunologydsa"       "infectionpathogen"  
#> [19] "infectionsite"       "organintervention"   "livertumormarkerlab"
#> [22] "livertumorstaging"   "livertumortherapy"   "lungfctassessment"  
#> [25] "lungfev1best"        "medicationtreatment" "organ"              
#> [28] "organevent"          "organlab"            "organlongitudinal"  
#> [31] "patient"             "patientdisease"      "patienthla"         
#> [34] "patientindex"        "patientlab"          "patientlongitudinal"
#> [37] "patientserology"     "perioperativecare"   "psq"                
#> [40] "psqadherence"        "psqdaysleep"         "psqeducation"       
#> [43] "psqequvas"           "psqquol"             "psqsleep"           
#> [46] "psqtrust"            "psq2exercise"        "psq2profession"     
#> [49] "psq2workcap"         "psq3activity"        "psq3household"      
#> [52] "psq3occupation"      "psq3sport"           "rejectiontreatment" 
#> [55] "stop"                "stimulationlab"      "transplantation"    
#> [58] "relisting"           "valuemetadata"       "virology"           
#> [61] "variablemetadata"

    NOTE: Data-cuts contain a subset of the previous tables, according to the project I/E criteria and aims.

    A specific table can be retrieved using the $ sign:

    stcs$patient |> 
  slice(0L)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 25
#> # ℹ 25 variables: patientkey <chr>, patid <chr>, enrollment_date <date>,
#> #   enrollment_age <int>, sex <chr>, bg <chr>, ethnicity <chr>, initials <chr>,
#> #   dob <date>, yob <int>, ethnicity_comment <chr>, istreat <chr>,
#> #   reconsent_candidate <chr>, reconsent_comment <chr>, creation_date <date>,
#> #   gwas_availability <chr>, gwas_date <date>, gwas_method <chr>,
#> #   pre_organ_count <int>, pre_tpx_count <int>, last_consent_date <date>,
#> #   last_consent_status <chr>, last_withdrawal_option <chr>, …

    In addition, there are 3 special tables that contain meta-information: Admin, VariableMetaData and ValueMetaData.

    3.2 The Admin table

    The Admin table contains information about the STCS export:

    stcs$admin
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   extraction_date cohort_startdate research_startdate first_extraction_datetime
#>   <date>          <date>           <date>             <dttm>                   
#> 1 2026-04-01      2008-01-01       2008-05-01         2026-04-01 01:25:00      
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: last_extraction_datetime <dttm>, processing_date <date>,
#> #   pkg_version <chr>, core_version <chr>

    3.3 VariableMetaData

    The VariableMetaData table contains information on each variable within each table:

    stcs$variablemetadata
#> # A tibble: 893 × 9
#>    dataset         dataset_pk variable   datatype organ_relevance stcs3lc_source
#>    <chr>           <chr>      <chr>      <chr>    <chr>           <chr>         
#>  1 Admin           NA         extractio… Date     Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  2 Admin           NA         cohort_st… Date     Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  3 Admin           NA         research_… Date     Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  4 Admin           NA         first_ext… Date-Ti… Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  5 Admin           NA         last_extr… Date-Ti… Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  6 Admin           NA         processin… Date     Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  7 Admin           NA         pkg_versi… Charact… Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  8 Admin           NA         core_vers… Charact… Heart - Islets… NA            
#>  9 AllCancerStatus NA         patientkey Charact… Heart - Islets… patient:patie…
#> 10 AllCancerStatus NA         diseasekey Charact… Heart - Islets… neoplasiastat…
#> # ℹ 883 more rows
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: historic_source <chr>, variable_description <chr>,
#> #   variable_values <chr>

    The column dataset_pk is of particular interest as it contains the unique identifier (eg: Primary Key) of each row of the table. For instance, patientkey and consent_date are, together, a unique identifier of the rows of stcs$consent:

    stcs$variablemetadata |> 
  select(dataset,dataset_pk) |> 
  distinct()
#> # A tibble: 60 × 2
#>    dataset         dataset_pk              
#>    <chr>           <chr>                   
#>  1 Admin           NA                      
#>  2 AllCancerStatus NA                      
#>  3 BiopsyRejection biorejkey               
#>  4 Biosample       biosampkey              
#>  5 BiosampleUsage  NA                      
#>  6 CareProvider    providerkey             
#>  7 Consent         patientkey, consent_date
#>  8 Donor           donorkey                
#>  9 DonorHLA        donorkey                
#> 10 DonorSerology   donorkey, test          
#> # ℹ 50 more rows

    3.4 ValueMetaData

    The ValueMetaData table contains information on each value (tables under construction):

    stcs$valuemetadata
#> # A tibble: 4,326 × 12
#>    dataset  variable datatype organ_relevance value_label value_name dataset_3lc
#>    <chr>    <chr>    <chr>    <chr>           <chr>       <chr>      <chr>      
#>  1 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… No          No         neoplasias…
#>  2 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… No          No         skincancer…
#>  3 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Yes         Yes        neoplasias…
#>  4 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Yes         Yes        skincancer…
#>  5 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Cured or r… Cured or … neoplasias…
#>  6 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Incident    Incident   neoplasias…
#>  7 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Incident    Incident   skincancer…
#>  8 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Loc progre… Local pro… skincancer…
#>  9 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Local recu… Local rec… skincancer…
#> 10 AllCanc… cancer_… chr      Heart - Islets… Newly dete… Newly det… neoplasias…
#> # ℹ 4,316 more rows
#> # ℹ 5 more variables: variable_3lc <chr>, is_ongoing <lgl>, period <chr>,
#> #   period_startdate <date>, period_stopdate <date>

    3.5 Searching a regular expression

    The stcs_search() function can be used to search a pattern in all variables in the stcs. It uses stringr::str_detect() to detect the filter the appropriate regular expression. When combined with stcs_select_table() the search is performed on a subset of tables.

    stcs |>
  stcs_select_table(tables = c("patientdisease", "infectionpathogen", "infectionsite")) |>
  stcs_search(fixed("bact", ignore_case = TRUE)) |> 
  arrange(desc(sapply(result, nrow))) |> 
  slice(0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 4
#> # ℹ 4 variables: dataset <chr>, variable <chr>, value <chr>, result <list>

    4 Tailored tables

    Tailored-tables are additional pre-programmed tables with derived variables.

    4.1 Baseline variable (BL)

    For baseline characteristics:

    patbl <- tailored_patientbl(stcs)
txbl <- tailored_transplantationbl(stcs)
# contains serology combination and HLA-mismatches
txbl |> 
  slice(0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 71
#> # ℹ 71 variables: soaskey <chr>, patientkey <chr>, donorkey <chr>,
#> #   organ_count <int>, tpx <chr>, tpx_resec <chr>, pre_tpxspecific_count <int>,
#> #   tpxspecific_order <int>, tpx_order <int>, tpx_stcsorder <int>,
#> #   abocomp <lgl>, hlaamismatch <int>, hlabmismatch <int>, hlacmismatch <int>,
#> #   hladpbmismatch <int>, hladqbmismatch <int>, hladrb1mismatch <int>,
#> #   hladrb35mismatch <int>, sumhlamismatch <int>, hlaavailable <int>,
#> #   procedure_provider <chr>, dontype <chr>, donrelsubtype <chr>, …

    NOTE: The variables of the tailored tables depend on the data-cut. For instance HLA-mismatches will only be available if the stcs$patienthla and stcs$donorhla tables are available in the data-cut.

    NOTE: The stcs$organ contains most organ-level baseline variable. In addition, “Baseline” has a different meaning for patients (time of enrollment/first STCS transplantation) and for transplants (time of transplantation).

    4.2 Events post BL

    “Survival” tailored tables contain important post-baseline dates, useful for time-to-event/survival analysis:

    patsurv <- tailored_patientsurvival(stcs)
orgsurv <- tailored_organsurvival(stcs)
txsurv <- tailored_transplantationsurvival(stcs)

    4.3 Wide PSQ

    In the data-cut, the PSQ tables are provided in long-format, allowing a full representation of the data. A merged version, in wide format, is available as follows:

    wpsq <- tailored_psq(stcs)

    5 Creating custom data-set

    In the next example, a diagnostic-level (diseasekey) dataset is created by including patient-level (patientkey) variables. First, we select identifiers from stcs$patientdisease. Then, the var_available() function displays which variables might be merged, given the -key in the data.

    stcs$patientdisease |>
  select(diseasekey,  patientkey, patdiagnosis, date) |>
  var_available(stcs)
#> Associate to key: patientkey 
#>  - In table: patient 
#>    bg, bl_consent_date, bl_consent_status, creation_date, dob, enrollment_age, 
#>    enrollment_date, ethnicity, ethnicity_comment, gwas_availability, gwas_date, 
#>    gwas_method, initials, istreat, last_consent_date, last_consent_status, 
#>    last_withdrawal_option, patid, pre_organ_count, pre_tpx_count, 
#>    reconsent_candidate, reconsent_comment, sex, yob
#> 
#>  - In table: patienthla 
#>    hlaa_0, hlaa_1, hlab_0, hlab_1, hlac_0, hlac_1, hladpb_0, hladpb_1, 
#>    hladqb_0, hladqb_1, hladrb1_0, hladrb1_1, hladrb35_0, hladrb35_1
#> 
#> 
#> Associate to key: diseasekey 
#>  - In table: patientdisease 
#>    cad_event, comment, confirmed_cause_id, confirmed_cause_ud, cvd_event, 
#>    dateaccuracy, donorrelid, hepb_course, hepc_course, histoid, hospreqid, 
#>    inftype, is_clt, is_cp, is_evdis, is_id, is_mek, is_neoplasia, is_pre, 
#>    is_pretx, is_skincancer, is_validated, isred, nbpromise, nosocomial, 
#>    organkey, pad_event, patid_old, ptld_subtype, rrt, smpcollection
#> 
#> 
#> Associate to key: patientkey, date 
#>  - In table: stop 
#>    autopsy, backstcs, backstcsdate, comment, crf_status, dateaccuracy, 
#>    deathcauseverified, dropoutreason, lastalivedate, out

    For each key (eg: patientkey, diseasekey and patientkey, date), the list of variable which can be join the the current data is displayed. Note the variables of the stcs$stop are proposed as patientkey, date is the unique identifier of stcs$stop and both variable name are available in the dataset. However, both date does not represent the same type of events (diagnostic VS stop), hence, merging using those two dates would not make sense.

    Once variables are chosen, add_var() is used to include it in the data. As patientkey is available in our data-set, all variables from stcs$patient might be added/join to our current data-set. Here, we simply add enrollment_age:

    stcs$patientdisease |> 
  select(diseasekey,  patientkey, patdiagnosis, date) |>
  add_var(stcs, c("enrollment_age")) |> 
  slice(0L)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: diseasekey <chr>, patientkey <chr>, patdiagnosis <chr>,
#> #   date <date>, enrollment_age <int>

    If the variable-name appears in several tables, the name of the table must be specified using the from = argument.

    # It produces an error as sex and bg are available for donor:
# stcs$patientdisease |> 
#   select(diseasekey,  patientkey, patdiagnosis, date) |>
#   add_var(stcs, c("enrollment_age", "sex", "bg")) |> 
#   slice(0L)

stcs$patientdisease |>
  select(diseasekey,  patientkey, patdiagnosis, date) |>
  add_var(stcs, c("enrollment_age", "rec_sex" = "sex", "bg"), from = "patient") |>
  slice(0L)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 7
#> # ℹ 7 variables: diseasekey <chr>, patientkey <chr>, patdiagnosis <chr>,
#> #   date <date>, enrollment_age <int>, rec_sex <chr>, bg <chr>

    6 Helper functions

    6.1 Missing type

    The is_truemissing() function is used to detect the Missing type and Missing can be set to NA using truemissing_to_na().

    v_chr <- c("data", "Missing", "again data")
v_dbl <- c(1, 2, -9999, -9998)
v_dt <- c(as.Date("1700-01-01"), as.Date("2020-12-25"))

is_truemissing(v_chr)
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
is_truemissing(v_dbl)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
is_truemissing(v_dt)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

    To set it as NA:

    truemissing_to_na(v_chr)
#> [1] "data"       NA           "again data"
truemissing_to_na(v_dbl)
#> [1]     1     2    NA -9998
truemissing_to_na(v_dt)
#> [1] NA           "2020-12-25"

    NOTE: The STCS does not contains Missing type for logical data-type.

    6.2 Value - comment pairs

    The paste_valuecomment() function is used to handle the “value - comment” pairs:

    paste_valuecomment(c("value1", "value2"), c(NA, "comment2"))
#> [1] "value1 | value2:comment2"

    For instance, it can be used to have infection-level data-set while keeping the infection-site information:

    stcs$infectionsite |> 
  slice(1:100) |> 
  summarise(
    infsite_n = n(),
    aggr_infiste = paste_valuecomment(infsite, comment),
    .by = diseasekey) |> 
  arrange(desc(infsite_n)) |> 
  slice(0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # ℹ 3 variables: diseasekey <chr>, infsite_n <int>, aggr_infiste <chr>

    6.3 Merging intervals

    The stcs$medicationtreatment contains interval data. Depending on the relevant categorization, they might overlap and merging it would be the first analysis step. In the following example, all periods of induction drugs are merged by patients. It would be useful to compute for instance the number of days with induction during the first months:

    # warning: this processing does not consider inaccuracy of date.
stcs$medicationtreatment |>
  filter(drug_category == "drug_ind") |>
  # NA stop-date are considered as ongoing treatment
  mutate(medication_startdate = replace_na(medication_stopdate, stcs$admin$extraction_date)) |>
  # Missing/NA stop and stop date are considered as data-entry error
  filter(!is.na(truemissing_to_na(medication_startdate))) |>
  filter(!is_truemissing(medication_stopdate)) |>
  filter(medication_stopdate >= medication_startdate) |>
  reframe(
    merge_intervals(medication_startdate, medication_stopdate, .lag = 1),
    .by = patientkey
  ) |>
  slice(0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 3
#> # ℹ 3 variables: patientkey <chr>, x0 <date>, x1 <date>

    6.4 Protocol date

    Only the actual date of assessment assdate is recorded in the STCS, however aligning the date to the expected date from the protocol is often useful. As there is an assessment at baseline, M6, Y1, Y2, …, one can use closest_value() for aligning the effective time to the protocol time. It can be done as follow:

    stcs$patientlongitudinal |> 
  left_join(
    summarise(stcs$organ, 
              tpxdate = min(tpxdate),
              .by = patientkey),
    by = "patientkey",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |> 
  select(patientkey, patlongkey, assdate, tpxdate) |> 
  mutate(eff_days = as.integer(assdate -tpxdate),
         pp_days = closest_value(eff_days, 
                                 target = round(c(0, 186, 365.25*c(1:25))))) |> 
  slice(0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 6
#> # ℹ 6 variables: patientkey <chr>, patlongkey <chr>, assdate <date>,
#> #   tpxdate <date>, eff_days <int>, pp_days <dbl>

    NOTE: They might be several assessments for the same pp_days as some events (eg: transplantation, death) trigger an assessment.

    6.5 First event

    The time-to-(first)-event variables are derived using base::pmin() (for the time) together with which.pmin_chr() (for the event). Here is simple example using 3 types of event:

    # time of event 
eventA <- c(1, 2, 3, 2)
eventB <- c(2, 1.5, NA, 2)
eventC <- c(NA, NA, 2, 3)

# time of first event 
pmin(eventA, eventA, eventC, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 2 2 2
# Which event come first? 
## In case of ties, display all.
which.pmin_chr(A = eventA, B = eventB, C = eventC, ties = "collapse")
#> [1] "A"     "B"     "C"     "A | B"
## In case of ties, choose according to the order in the function.
which.pmin_chr(A = eventA, B = eventB, C = eventC, ties = "first")
#> [1] "A" "B" "C" "A"
which.pmin_chr(B = eventB, A = eventA, C = eventC, ties = "first")
#> [1] "A" "B" "C" "B"

    7 Use case: Kaplan-Meier

    Combining the previous functions, the Kaplan-Meier estimator of the patient survival is derived as follow:

    tb_km <- 
  # Use the tailored "survival" table
  patsurv |> 
  select(patientkey, enrollment_date, first_dropoutdate, 
         last_assdate, last_consent_withdrawal_date, deathdate,
         extraction_date) |> 
  # Only select patients with consent (last known value)
  add_var(stcs, "last_consent_status") |> 
  filter(last_consent_status == "Present") |> 
  # Last-assessment should not censored the terminal event
  mutate(last_assdate = replace(last_assdate, !is.na(deathdate), NA)) |> 
  # Compute time to death, censoring for dropout, last-assessment, 
  # consent withdrawal and STCS data extraction date.
  mutate(
    event_date = pmin(
      deathdate, first_dropoutdate, last_assdate, 
      last_consent_withdrawal_date, extraction_date,  
      na.rm = TRUE),
    event_chr = which.pmin_chr(
      death = deathdate, cens = first_dropoutdate, cens = last_assdate,
      cens = last_consent_withdrawal_date, cens = extraction_date,
      ties = "first")) |> 
  mutate(event_01 = as.integer(event_chr == "death"),
         event_days = as.integer(event_date -enrollment_date))

km <- survfit(Surv(event_days, event_01) ~ 1, data = tb_km)
plot(km)
